fr:frontmatter.fr:meta: @misc{yeFlashInferEfficientCustomizable2025, title = {{{FlashInfer}}: {{Efficient}} and {{Customizable Attention Engine}} for {{LLM Inference Serving}}}, author = {Ye, Zihao and Chen, Lequn and Lai, Ruihang and Lin, Wuwei and Zhang, Yineng and Wang, Stephanie and Chen, Tianqi and Kasikci, Baris and Grover, Vinod and Krishnamurthy, Arvind and Ceze, Luis}, year = {2025}, doi = {10.48550/arXiv.2501.01005}, urldate = {2026-08-21}, number = {arXiv:2501.01005}, publisher = {arXiv}, file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/FlashInfer Efficient and Customizable Attention Engine for LLM Inference Serving - Ye et al..pdf}, keywords = {Computer Science - Artificial Intelligence,Computer Science - Distributed Parallel and Cluster Computing,Computer Science - Machine Learning}, archiveprefix = {arXiv}, abstract = {Transformers, driven by attention mechanisms, form the foundation of large language models (LLMs). As these models scale up, efficient GPU attention kernels become essential for high-throughput and low-latency inference. Diverse LLM applications demand flexible and high-performance attention solutions. We present FlashInfer: a customizable and efficient attention engine for LLM serving. FlashInfer tackles KV-cache storage heterogeneity using block-sparse format and composable formats to optimize memory access and reduce redundancy. It also offers a customizable attention template, enabling adaptation to various settings through Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation. Additionally, FlashInfer's load-balanced scheduling algorithm adjusts to dynamism of user requests while maintaining compatibility with CUDAGraph which requires static configuration. FlashInfer have been integrated into leading LLM serving frameworks like SGLang, vLLM and MLC-Engine. Comprehensive kernel-level and end-to-end evaluations demonstrate FlashInfer's ability to significantly boost kernel performance across diverse inference scenarios: compared to state-of-the-art LLM serving solutions, FlashInfer achieve 29-69\% inter-token-latency reduction compared to compiler backends for LLM serving benchmark, 28-30\% latency reduction for long-context inference, and 13-17\% speedup for LLM serving with parallel generation.}, primaryclass = {cs.DC}, eprint = {2501.01005}, month = {April}, shorttitle = {{{FlashInfer}}} }

fr:title.text: POTW: 🎂 CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: POTW: 🎂 CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Problem. In this paper, they aim to address the problem of agentic kernel generation or as we refer to it: vibe compilation. Specifically, they target CUDA and raw PTX as a backend.
Technical challenges. There are many issues that arise in vibe compilation. A non-exhaustive list of challenges is as follows:

html:ul.html:li: Reward Hacking: A very common theme for any reinforcement learning based approach. In particular, see this paper for some examples of agents hacking KernelBench.

Synchronization errors: Even given a list of input output examples to check against, we cannot possibly determine whether there is an underlying race condition that appears rarely enough to pass the checks.
This seems to be a main focus of things like TIRx, where they hope to check these things at the IR level.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Core contribution. They develop CAKE IR, which is an intermediate representation for writing CUDA kernels. More importantly, they have the agent co-design the IR while trying to generate kernels. This is an iterative process, where the agent must implement existing kernels in its own designed IR. To do so, requires adding necessary features to the IR like Warp Specialization along with the corresponding lowering passes.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Starting bare IR. The agent is then given a warp-specialized kernel and sees that it needs to add support for warp specialization via lm.role

fr:mainmatter.html:p: They can then iteratively build on this pipeline adding architecture specific features. For example, the IR example they give shows that they have an lm.tmem API for TMEM. This can be thought of as a v3 given below.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Building on the IR with Warp Specialization. Add support for architecture specific features like TMEM as the candles on top of the IR

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How this is actually implemented is a trade secretI suspect one reason that a lot of this is not publicly available is that it is only understood by GPT 5.6.
Evaluation. They evaluate against (their own) well-tuned kernels from FlashInfer.

Where they might struggle. It is unclear how well this would work for ASICs like TPUs or Trainium. I suspect that in order to "converge" to a good IR, you need to reduce the degrees of freedom through a large number of kernel examples. The kernel ecosystem of these accelerators is far less mature, making it much harder to extract useful abstractions.
I believe the layering analogy was meant as adding increasingly specific features, but I wonder whether a vibe MLIR could be developed to allow other accelerators to inherit some of the benefits.
Most of the work in this paper is not publicly available, so I have a lot of outstanding questions.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. What are the exact input / outputs in IR developement and during search?
fr:mainmatter.html:p: For the IR, they have "IR principles"

My best guess is that the workflow is roughly 1. prepend these principles to the input via some prompt 2. provide new kernel(s) that likely require some new abstraction and 3. have GPT vibe code IR updates.
